extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic and the philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing the warrant, scope, and methods of inductive inferences about uniformities of succession and co-existence in nature. Emphasizes when simple enumeration suffices, how scientific induction improves it, and limits of claiming universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief in universal causation is itself an induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The belief in the universality of the law of cause and effect is an instance of induction, derived by generalizing from many particular cases of causation or partial uniformities of sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat the law of causation as an a priori certainty; it was inferred from observed partial uniformities. Its status is established by generalization from many observed causal cases, and thus any evaluation of inferences should recognize this foundational inductive origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status and limits of simple enumeration (per enumerationem simplicem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction by simple enumeration—generalization from the mere absence of any known contrary instance—is a valid but fallible form of induction and often the only kind possible initially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize simple enumeration affords some practical assurance (e.g., 'food nourishes'), but is precarious especially for narrow, special subject-matters. Prefer replacing it with less fallible methods when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific induction improves simple enumeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific induction substitutes operations grounded in the same basic process but in less fallible forms; it tests and corrects inartificial generalizations by means of stronger inductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To improve a generalization, show it follows from or conflicts with some stronger induction (a broader generalization resting on a larger foundation of experience). This testing is the core logic of induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale of trustworthiness depends on breadth of generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The precariousness of simple enumeration is inversely proportional to the largeness/general scope of the generalization: broader generalizations (covering wide subject-matter) are less liable to mislead than very special ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give greater credence to wide-ranging empirical generalizations (e.g., principles of number, geometry, law of causation) derived by enumeration than to narrow ones; evaluate narrow generalizations more critically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical laws are valid only within observed limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A generalization observed repeatedly and without known exception may be taken as an empirical law true within certain limits of time, place, and circumstance, provided coincidences exceed what could be attributed to chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not extend such generalizations beyond those limits without further evidence — exceptions may arise from local collocations or counteracting agencies. Measure strength by how unlikely an exception could have remained unobserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of causation as the most universal and sanctioning induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of causation is the most universal observed uniformity and can impart certainty to other inductive propositions when those propositions can be connected to it; it thereby increases their evidential weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer connecting narrower inferences to the law of causation to render them more certain. Treat subordinate generalizations as proved only insofar as they are consistent with or deducible from causal laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical entitlement to disregard crude enumeration when causal confirmation exists
rubrics_metrics.description: When a generalization can be shown to be consistent with, or follow from, the law of causation via the Four Methods, we are logically entitled to ignore the lesser probabilities produced by crude early generalizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate minor generalizations primarily by whether the law of causation confirms them; do not rely on the probabilities from initial simple enumeration alone if causal methods can be applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution of apparent circularity between induction and law of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparent paradox that inductions assume the law of causation while the law itself is a product of induction is resolved by recognizing both general and particular truths are proved from the same body of experience rather than one proving the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess inferences by their common evidential base; accept that both general laws and particular conclusions derive warrant directly from experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical completeness of the law of causation within experience
rubrics_metrics.description: For practical purposes within the range of human experience (e.g., within the solar system), the law of uniform succession may be regarded as complete and conclusive, though not warranting extension beyond observable domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat causal uniformities as virtually certain within well-observed domains, but avoid asserting universal, domain-transcending laws without additional evidence; be cautious about extrapolation to radically different conditions (e.g., distant stellar regions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between uniformities of succession and co-existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities in nature are of two kinds: succession (temporal order, governed by causation) and co-existence (simultaneity), and they have different epistemic grounds and methods of investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use causal methods (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations) for sequences/succession. Do not assume the same methods apply to co-existence; treat the two classes separately when evaluating generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-existences between ultimate properties cannot depend on causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-existences among ultimate properties (those not caused by anything else) cannot be explained by causation; if such co-existences are true, they indicate ultimate properties of a single Kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating assertions about properties of Kinds, distinguish whether properties are ultimate (intrinsic to Kind) or derivative (effects of causes). If ultimate, their co-existence is a different epistemic problem than causal inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizations about Kinds are uniformities of co-existence and lack a causal axiom
rubrics_metrics.description: Any proposition about the properties of a Kind (e.g., 'All crows are black') asserts uniformity of co-existence; unlike succession, there is no general axiom (analogous to causation) to ground elimination methods for such propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because elimination methods (Agreement, Difference) are inapplicable, generalizations about Kinds must be assessed by other means (notably the improbability that an exception would have remained unobserved). Be wary of applying Baconian elimination uncritically to co-existences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of certainty for co-existence generalizations measured by improbability of unobserved exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The certainty of a generalization resting solely on past agreement of observation is measured by the improbability that an exception, if it exists, could until now have remained unobserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast claims like 'All crows are black' as questions about how unlikely it is that non-black crows exist without detection. Use this improbability-as-evidence heuristic to judge the strength of such generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two epistemic possibilities for a property observed in a Kind
rubrics_metrics.description: If a property (e.g., blackness in crows) is observed universally, either it is accidental (an effect produced by causes and therefore an empirical law) or it is a property of Kind (ultimate), implying the possible discovery of a distinct Kind if exceptions are found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate which possibility is more plausible: if variability or causal influence is plausible (especially in organisms), treat the property as derivative and seek causal explanations; if treated as ultimate, acknowledge that new Kinds might exist and that certainty is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organized beings' properties are presumptively derivative and thus empirical
rubrics_metrics.description: Organized beings (animals, plants, humans) are highly modifiable and have beginnings (causes), so their properties are likely derivative (effects of causes) rather than ultimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing generalizations about living organisms, favor causal explanations and empirical induction; expect more variability and be cautious about asserting immutable properties of kinds in biology or similar domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of new Kinds limits certainty of co-existence generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Because new Kinds (species, minerals, etc.) are continually detected, often in well-explored areas, generalizations about co-existence (properties of Kinds) cannot attain absolute certainty and must remain empirical at best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain epistemic humility about universal claims regarding Kinds; account for the reasonable possibility of overlooked or undiscovered Kinds when judging strength of such claims.
